title: Population and sample; random, stratified and convenience sampling

videos.script: Until now the course described the data in front of it. Twelve orders, four hundred baskets. What they were, and nothing more. {{described}} From this lesson on, the question changes. The data is a small part of something larger, and you want to say something about the larger thing. {{larger}} Horta cannot ask all of its customers whether they like the new app. It asks some of them, and hopes the answer holds for the rest. {{some}} Whether it does depends almost entirely on how the some were chosen. {{chosen}} Choose them at random, and the answer wobbles a little from sample to sample, by an amount you can measure. Choose them in groups that mirror the population, and it wobbles less. {{random}} Choose them because they were easy to reach, and the answer can be wrong in a way that no amount of extra data will fix. {{easy}} This lesson is about those choices. It ends with a famous poll that asked more than two million people and still got the election badly wrong. {{poll}}
